8.1: Seven finished books stood in the library. The atlas lay open to a blank page beside three invitations: a sunny meadow for a picnic or flower viewing, a broad pine lookout for sketching, and a dry reed-bank platform for sharing a book. Lark made room beside her. This time the purpose and destination belonged to your choice.

“We can read to choose something we want to do,” Lark explained warmly. “Sun has our short u, pine has long i with final e, and reed has ee. Read the three labels, then connect each one to its offered purpose. None is a better reading answer.”
“Which outing would you like to plan, and what would you like to do there?” Lark asked gently. “You can point, tell us, or use the invitation pictures.”

Lark entered the selected invitation in the destination space on the atlas draft. The other invitations stayed available for another day. Choosing a route did not claim the crew had visited it yet. Nib set out three more spaces beside it: equipment, stopping place, and a useful condition or alternative.
The sun is up. The pine is tall. The reed is by the bank.
“Which sentence connects the reed to a place?” Lark asked gently. “Which invitation fits your own purpose?”

Your first atlas journal page would keep the actual route and purpose you selected. A second source waited for each possible outing, ready to add preparation information the cheerful invitation had left out.

sun: The meadow invitation promised space to enjoy a picnic or look at flowers. Its second page showed a shade cloth and a mat. Nib brought a whole tower of workshop boxes. Lark put the equipment page beside the four planning spaces and waited to see what the outing actually required.

“A second source can add something the first leaves out,” Lark explained gently. “Read its preparation words, then connect them to your chosen purpose. We need a reason for each item, not every item that happens to fit in a bag.”
“Read the meadow equipment passage,” Lark invited gently. “Which two things serve this outing?”

Nib returned the workshop boxes. The shade cloth and mat went into the kit, with their attachment pieces packed beside them. Lark left the destination in its own space and added the actual equipment to the next. The page had improved the same meadow plan rather than sending the crew on a different outing.
mat
Pack the mat. Pack the shade cloth.
“Which two things does the page ask us to pack?” Lark asked gently.
Your meadow draft now named its useful kit. If a word or instruction still needed help, the same page would remain available before anyone had to explain the plan.
pine: The pine invitation offered a broad lookout for sketching. A second page pictured a light coat and sketch board. Nib brought several picnic baskets instead. Lark laid the preparation note beside the selected purpose so the equipment could serve the drawing trip.

“A second source can supply missing preparation,” Lark explained gently. “Read the equipment words and connect them to the sketching purpose. The right kit is the one with a reason to come, rather than the largest pile we can carry.”
“Read the pine equipment passage,” Lark invited gently. “Which items belong to the planned sketching stop?”

Nib packed the light coat and sketch board, leaving unrelated baskets at camp. Lark recorded that actual kit in the second planning space. The pine route stayed selected. The crew had learned more about the same outing, not completed it by packing.
coat
Pack the coat. Pack the sketch board.
“Which items does this page ask us to bring?” Lark asked gently.
Your pine draft now included its useful kit. The direction page could be revisited with whatever support made it understandable before the crew summarized the plan.
reed: The reed invitation promised a quiet waterside book stop on a dry platform. Its second page showed a protective book cover and mat. Nib reached for the workshop's heavy tool chest. Lark held the book page beside the actual purpose of the trip.

“A second source adds preparation to the invitation,” Lark explained gently. “Read the equipment words, then ask how each thing helps our book stop. We can supply an unfamiliar topic word without pretending it was read independently.”
“Read the reed equipment passage,” Lark invited gently. “What protects the book, and what gives us a place to settle?”

Nib packed the dry cover and mat, with the chosen book protected inside its folio. The heavy tool chest stayed in the workshop. Lark entered the equipment in its own planning space. A waterside plan could be pleasant and still account carefully for keeping paper dry.
cover
Pack the dry cover. Pack the mat.
“Which packed item protects the book?” Lark asked gently.
Your reed draft held its purpose and useful kit. The dry-cover instruction remained available if anyone wanted to hear, decode, or discuss part of it again.

sun: The meadow page stayed open beside the packed shade cloth. Lark left room to mark any actual uncertainty about its words or shade placement. Nib did not invent a hard word for you. If everything already made sense, the crew could simply keep using the page.

“Help can answer different needs,” Lark explained warmly. “We can hear a sound or chunk, discuss a meaning, or replay the relevant sentence. Choose what would help with your actual question, or continue without help if you don't need it.”
“Is there a part of this shade instruction you want help with?” Lark asked gently.

Any chosen support would stay attached to the same passage. Lark could model a needed part, then invite a reread in context. The planning space would be settled when the information made sense, with whatever support had been used. Nobody had to demonstrate a difficulty to continue.
a useful word from your page
The shade is by the path. The mat can sit in the shade.
“Where can the mat go?” Lark asked gently. “Which words help you decide?”
Your meadow plan kept its shaded placement. The next job was telling the crew the information in an order they could use.
pine: A direction phrase on the pine page could be marked if it caused real uncertainty. Lark kept its diagram beside the sentence. Nib waited with the sketch board instead of reading the answer over your shoulder. If the direction was already clear, no help ritual was needed.

“Choose support for the part you actually need,” Lark offered warmly. “A sound model helps decode; a meaning explanation helps understand; a replay helps reconnect the sentence. You may also continue unaided. The point is using the page, not proving you can refuse help.”
“Would any part of the pine direction benefit from a model, explanation, or replay?” Lark asked gently.

Lark would use the chosen support on the actual phrase, then return to its meaning in the plan. The selected pine outing and equipment remained in view. A supported reading could guide a useful trip just as a reading without help could.
a useful direction word
The pine is by the hut. The path is wide.
“What does the page say about the path?” Lark asked gently.
Your pine plan kept the understood direction with its source. The crew would next need that information explained in a clear order.
reed: The dry-cover instruction stayed beside the reed route's packed book. Lark offered space to mark any real question about it. Nib left the cover open for inspection. Nobody pretended you had struggled with a word before you had even tried it.

“Help should fit the question,” Lark explained warmly. “We can model a sound or chunk, explain a meaning, or replay the relevant sentence. Or we can continue without help. We'll keep the actual source visible so the support changes what you can use.”
“Is any part of the cover instruction unclear?” Lark asked gently. “Choose help only if it would be useful.”

Any requested model or explanation would return to the same book-cover instruction. Lark would invite a reread and check what the instruction meant for the packed book. Whatever support was used, the purpose remained sharing the book on the dry platform.
a useful cover word
The book is in the dry cover. The mat is by the kit.
“What keeps the book dry in this passage?” Lark asked gently.
Your reed plan kept the cover instruction understood. Next the crew needed your explanation, with words, pictures, or dictation all available.

sun: Lark summarized the meadow plan and put the shade behind the packed kit instead of where it would cover the mat. She held the source beside her summary so the difference could be checked. Nib waited to learn which practical job would help.

“An explanation needs a useful order,” Lark explained gently. “Read first, then, and last. Use the source to tell us the destination and kit, and show where the shade belongs. Your actual words or arranged pictures can become our draft.”
“Tell us the meadow plan so we can take useful jobs,” Lark invited warmly. “What needs correcting in my summary?”

Lark kept the atlas draft open for your explanation instead of substituting a canned sentence. Nib could take the shade-packing job while Lark checked the route source. The crew's jobs would follow the explained plan. Its next related page would add a condition the first invitation had not discussed.
one part of your own summary
First pack the mat. Then pack the shade.
“Which packing job comes first in this example?” Lark asked gently.
The meadow summary kept what you actually explained. A separate condition space stayed empty until the next relevant source was read.
pine: Lark's pine summary put the sketch board into the route bag but forgot the place to pause and use it. She set the source beside that incomplete summary. Nib held the board ready, waiting for a job that belonged to the actual sketching plan.

“Tell information in an order someone can use,” Lark explained gently. “First, then, and last can organize the explanation. Use the source to name the destination, kit, and planned pause. You can speak, arrange pictures, or dictate.”
“Explain the pine plan and check my summary,” Lark invited warmly. “Where should the board be used?”

The draft stayed open for your real explanation. Nib could pack and carry the board while Lark checked the direction source. Their tasks would come from the plan rather than silent corrections. The pine outing remained yours, with a later source still needed for its condition space.
one word from your own summary
First pack the board. Then pack the coat.
“Which item is packed after the board in this example?” Lark asked gently.
Your pine summary kept the order you explained. The next page would discuss a condition that affected the stopping place without replacing the chosen sketching purpose.
reed: Lark's reed summary put the mat into its cover and left the book uncovered. She brought the source closer so you could check the two jobs. Nib waited beside the actual dry book cover, ready to take a useful packing task.

“Explain the plan so another person can act on it,” Lark invited warmly. “Read first, then, and last. Use the source to show what stays dry and how. You can speak, arrange the pictures, or dictate your own explanation.”
“Check my summary and explain the book's protection,” Lark asked gently. “Which thing belongs in the dry cover?”

The atlas draft remained open for your actual explanation. Nib could take the cover-and-book job while Lark checked the path information. The crew would follow the same understood plan. A condition affecting the waterside stop still needed its own source.
a word from your actual explanation
First cover the book. Then pack the mat.
“What happens to the book before the mat is packed?” Lark asked gently.
Your reed summary kept the plan you explained. The final condition space stayed available for information about the bank and its dry alternative.

sun: The next meadow page compared the sunny clearing with its shaded edge. The first invitation had shown cheerful sunshine, but a comfortable stop needed more than a bright picture. Nib held the mat in the middle of the sun while Lark read the additional condition.

“A related source can qualify an earlier plan,” Lark explained thoughtfully. “Compare its information with your purpose. We don't have to abandon the meadow to use its shaded edge; we can keep the outing and improve where we stop.”
“Read the meadow condition,” Lark invited gently. “Which stop fits the purpose while allowing shade?”

The atlas draft could name the shaded edge instead of an exposed patch in the clearing. Nib kept the shade cloth with the mat. Lark left the reason beside the revision so another reader could understand it. The condition space now had information rather than a guess based on the invitation's mood.
shade
The sun is on the mat. The shade is by the path.
“Where does the passage put the shade?” Lark asked gently.
Your meadow plan could now be read as a whole: destination, equipment, and a reason for the shaded stop. A longer page would connect the approach with that final place.
pine: A related pine page compared an exposed viewpoint with a sheltered platform. Nib admired the open view, then caught the edge of his sketch paper as it lifted in the breeze. Lark set the wind information beside the original sketching purpose.

“Compare the second topic with the first purpose,” Lark explained gently. “A wind condition can change the stopping place without changing our interest in sketching. Keep the relevant words in the reason for the revised plan.”
“Read the pine condition,” Lark invited gently. “Which platform gives the sketch board a sheltered place?”

The draft could choose the sheltered viewing platform while keeping the pine lookout and sketching purpose. Nib packed the light coat and board together. Lark recorded why an exposed spot might be less useful for loose paper. The condition became part of the plan instead of an unwelcome surprise at the end.
wind
The wind is by the pine. The shelter has a wide platform.
“Which place has the wide platform?” Lark asked gently.
Your pine plan now included a condition and a suitable alternative within the same outing. The longer combined page would need both its approach paragraph and its stopping-place paragraph.
reed: The reed condition page showed a wet bank beside a dry boardwalk platform. The pleasant waterside invitation had not discussed where to set a paper book after rain. Nib kept the protected volume off the ground while Lark compared the two stopping places.

“Use the new topic to qualify the first plan,” Lark explained gently. “A wet bank doesn't mean abandoning our book stop. Read for the dry alternative and keep the reason attached to it, so another reader can make the same useful choice.”
“Read the bank condition,” Lark invited gently. “Which supported place keeps the reading stop dry?”

The draft could name the dry boardwalk platform. The cover and mat stayed in the kit, ready for the same chosen book purpose. Lark recorded the wet-bank reason beside the alternative. The creek did not need a new boat crossing for this plan; the dry supported route was already shown.
wet
The bank is wet. The platform is dry.
“Which place is dry?” Lark asked gently. “What does the other sentence tell us to account for?”
Your reed plan now held the relevant condition. The longer page would connect the dry approach and the actual supported reading stop.

sun: The meadow page had two short paragraphs. Nib read the approach and began to fold the plan shut. Lark put a wing beside the second paragraph. Arriving at the clearing was not the same as choosing the shaded edge where the outing would work comfortably.

“Read a longer page in manageable parts,” Lark invited warmly. “Pause after a paragraph, keep its meaning, then read the next. You can ask for a shorter span or help. We need both approach and stop, not a long performance for its own sake.”
“Use both paragraphs to choose our actual meadow stop,” Lark invited gently. “What does the second add?”

The draft would connect the broad dry approach with the shaded-edge stop. Nib checked that the mat and shade cloth matched that place. All four planning spaces could now be filled from actual sources. One fresh note remained to check a current condition before the outing.
stop

Follow the wide path. Stop in the shade.

Set the mat in the shade. Keep the path dry.
“Where do we stop after following the path?” Lark asked gently. “Which paragraph adds what to do there?”
Your meadow draft was complete enough to use. Its current condition would be checked once more before anyone led the real walk.
pine: The pine page's first paragraph described the path to the lookout. Nib started choosing a view before the second paragraph was read. Lark left the page open. Its next section described the sheltered platform where a board could rest level.

“Keep meaning across short sections,” Lark explained warmly. “Read a paragraph, pause, then connect the next one. A shorter span or help is available. Our job is to use the whole relevant page, not read for as long as possible.”
“Read both paragraphs,” Lark invited gently. “Which stop does the complete pine page identify?”

The draft would join the approach to the sheltered level platform. The coat and sketch board fitted that actual stop. Nib kept the plan open long enough to check the final line. The four information spaces were filled; a fresh note would still provide one current check.
platform

Follow the wide pine path. Pass the hut.

Stop on the sheltered platform. Set the board on the rest.
“Where should the board rest?” Lark asked gently. “Which paragraph supplies that final stopping information?”
Your pine plan now included the useful stopping place as well as the approach. A new note could confirm or revise one current detail before the sketching outing.
reed: The reed page began with the boardwalk approach. Nib started toward the nearest bank picture before Lark showed the second paragraph. The complete page led to the fixed dry reading platform, where the book could stay supported beside the water.

“Read the relevant sections together,” Lark invited warmly. “We can pause between paragraphs or shorten a span. Keep what the first part says, then let the next part add to it. Reading longer only helps when the information stays useful.”
“Use both paragraphs to find the actual reed stop,” Lark invited gently. “What does the second say about the book?”

The draft would connect the dry boardwalk to its fixed platform and book rest. The protective cover and mat matched that place. All four information spaces were filled. The last fresh note would check a current condition without replacing the chosen book outing.
path

Follow the dry path. Pass the reed bank.

Stop on the dry platform. Set the book on the fixed rest.
“Where should the book be set?” Lark asked gently. “Which paragraph gives the supported stop?”
Your reed plan now held the approach and exact reading place. One fresh note remained before the crew followed it on the real outing.

sun: The new meadow note stayed face down until your first attempt. Nib waited beside the actual mat and shade cloth. Lark kept the prepared plan nearby without reading the new answer aloud. The outing would remain available whether the note needed help or not.

“Use familiar spellings on this fresh note,” Lark invited warmly. “Try it before a model. Then decide whether its information changes the mat's place or our preparation. We can look at the real scene after the reading.”
“Read today's meadow note,” Lark invited gently. “Does its information call for moving the mat into shade?”

After the attempt, the crew could compare the note with the mat's real position and the shaded-edge plan. Any needed help would stay attached to the same text. Nib would carry the preparation agreed from that reading, without an accuracy threshold deciding whether the outing could happen.
mat
The mat is in the sun. The shade is by the path.
“Where is the mat now?” Lark asked gently. “How does that compare with the planned stop?”
Your meadow plan was ready for actual use, with its final decision tied to the fresh note. The next chapter would follow the child's directions rather than announce an outing that had not happened.
pine: The new pine note lay unopened beside the route plan. Nib waited with the sketch board while Lark left the answer unspoken. The coat remained packed. A fresh note could help a supported reader lead a real trip; it was not a last test to earn permission.

“Try the new note using familiar spellings,” Lark invited warmly. “Then compare its information with our prepared approach. Ask for help if a part needs it. We'll check the real scene only after giving the text its own reading.”
“Read today's pine note,” Lark invited gently. “Does it support our approach or change it?”

After the attempt, the crew could compare the note with the actual pine, hut, and wide path. Lark would record any help honestly. The plan could be confirmed or revised from its information. Nib kept the board ready for the selected supported platform.
pine
The pine is by the hut. The path is wide.
“What does the note say about the path?” Lark asked gently. “Does that fit the approach we prepared?”
Your pine plan was ready for use. The outing would follow the actual decision made from the note, with support still available while the child led.
reed: The new reed note remained covered while Nib held the protected book. Lark set the prepared dry-platform plan beside it without reading the new answer aloud. The boat mentioned in a note could be observed from the bank; it did not turn this chosen boardwalk outing into an unplanned crossing.

“Read the fresh note before a model,” Lark invited warmly. “Then decide what it changes, if anything, about the dry stopping place. Help is available. We will compare the actual scene after the text has had its first reading.”
“Read today's reed note,” Lark invited gently. “Which information matters to where we set the book?”

After the attempt, the crew could check the wet bank and the dock from dry ground. The selected book stop remained on its supported platform unless the actual reading gave a reason to revise it. Needed support would be recorded as support, with no invented independent result.
bank
The bank is wet. The boat is at the dock.
“Which sentence matters most to keeping a book off wet ground?” Lark asked gently.
Your reed plan was ready for the real outing. Nib would take the assigned book-cover job while Lark followed the child's directions along the supported dry approach.

sun: The meadow plan lay ready with its actual destination, kit, shaded stop, and condition. Lark moved beside you, prepared to follow the first direction. Nib carried the mat and shade cloth in the practical role agreed earlier. The atlas still had room for corrections from what the outing really showed.

“Lead us using the plan you made,” Lark invited warmly. “We can help read or check a detail. At the stop, compare the page with the real place. A useful atlas records what we actually find, including anything that needs changing.”
“Give our first direction, then check the shaded-edge stop against the page,” Lark invited gently.

At the shaded edge, Nib spread the mat on dry ground and fixed the shade cloth to its supports. The crew had time for the picnic or flower viewing you had chosen at the start. Lark checked the real approach against the page. Back at camp, she laid the draft beside your observations for approval and corrections. Nib set the approved source, paper, and ink on the portable press. A new atlas page emerged from the real materials.
a word from your approved page
The mat is in the shade. The path is dry.
“What does this example tell the next visitor about the mat and path?” Lark asked gently.

Lark placed the checked meadow entry in the atlas. Its destination, kit, shaded stop, and condition belonged to the outing just completed. Your explorer badge settled into the collection case. The Atlas We Make joined the seven earlier books. The meadow visit had its own finished ending; other invitations remained free choices for another day.
pine: The pine plan lay ready with its equipment, sheltered platform, and current condition. Lark stood beside you to follow the first direction. Nib took the assigned sketch-board job. The page would be checked against the actual view rather than presented as a perfect atlas before the crew had used it.

“Use your plan to lead the outing,” Lark invited warmly. “We can support a word or check a detail with you. At the platform, compare the real approach, stopping place, and equipment with the page. Corrections make a route more useful to its next reader.”
“Give the first pine direction and check our platform against the plan,” Lark invited gently.

At the sheltered level platform, Nib set the sketch board on its support. The light coat stayed ready as planned. There was time to make the chosen lookout sketch and compare the real approach with the page. Back at camp, Lark laid the draft beside your observations for approval and corrections. Nib prepared the approved source, paper, and ink. The press made a page from that real account, without claiming the untaken routes had been visited.
a word from your approved entry
The board is on the rest. The platform is dry.
“What does the example tell a sketching visitor about the stop?” Lark asked gently.

The checked pine entry and actual sketch took their places in the atlas. Your explorer badge marked the shared project. Lark bound The Atlas We Make and placed it beside the seven earlier books. The lookout outing was finished, its page ready for another reader. You could choose another book or route whenever you wished.
reed: The reed plan was ready beside the protected book. Lark waited to follow the first direction. Nib took the agreed cover-and-book job while the mat stayed packed for the dry platform. The real outing would check the page before it was approved for another reader.

“Lead us with the information you gathered,” Lark invited warmly. “Ask for help wherever it is useful. At the reading stop, compare the actual dry approach and fixed rest with the plan. The final atlas should keep your checked account rather than an invented perfect trip.”
“Give our first reed direction, then check the dry platform against the page,” Lark invited gently.

At the dry platform, Nib set the book on the fixed ledge and spread the mat. The crew shared the quiet reading chosen at the start. The cover stayed ready to protect the book again. Back at camp, Lark laid the draft beside the real observations for approval and corrections. Nib set the approved source, paper, and ink on the press. The atlas page came from that checked account, with no other route claimed as visited.
a word from your approved entry
The book is on the dry rest. The cover is by the mat.
“Where does this example keep the book?” Lark asked gently. “What remains ready beside the mat?”

The checked reed entry joined the atlas, giving another reader the dry approach, useful kit, supported stop, and wet-bank alternative. Your explorer badge settled beside the earlier keepsakes. The Atlas We Make joined the library as the eighth finished book. The waterside outing was complete, and the crew was free to choose another story without a new locked mystery.
